h: Geology and eruptions of Mount Karthala
x: A young and very active shield volcano: more than twenty eruptions in two centuries, some of which reached the sea, destroyed a village or covered Moroni in ash. Formation

Karthala is a shield volcano , like those of Hawaii or Piton de la Fournaise on Réunion: thousands of fluid basalt flows, stacked on top of each other, have built a relief with long, regular slopes, about 30 km long and 15 km wide. Eruptions do not only come out of the summit. The volcano is crossed by two fissure zones (“rifts”): one stretches 25 km to the north, the other 12 km to the south-east. Magma can force its way through them and open a fissure halfway down the slope, or even close to the coast. To the north, Karthala leans against another, older and less active volcano, La Grille , which forms the north of the island. Why a volcano here? Geologists still debate the origin of the Comoros: a hotspot, as on Réunion, or fractures in the plate that let magma rise. One thing is certain: Grande Comore is the youngest and most active of the four islands of the archipelago.

At the summit, the caldera measures about 3 km by 4. It is not a single crater but a set of nested collapses, which occurred when magma drained from beneath the summit. Two main craters open inside it: the Choungou Chahalé , in the centre: about 1,300 m long, 800 m wide and 300 m deep. This is the one you see from the caldera rim; the Choungou Changomeni , further north. The floor of the Chahalé changes with every eruption: a lake appeared after 1991 and disappeared in April 2005, then lava lakes formed and solidified there in 2006 and 2007.

Most Karthala eruptions are effusive : lava fountains and flows, not very explosive, with a Volcanic Explosivity Index of 0 to 2. Two notable exceptions, in 1918 and November 2005, threw ash over much of the island. Another danger is less visible: when groundwater meets the heat of the volcano, it can cause a phreatic explosion , as in 1991. Timeline

h: Two centuries of eruptions: the key dates
x: A selection, not a complete list: the volcano has erupted more than twenty times since 1828, and at least 34 times in the last 10,000 years. The latest alert was in 2022. Around 1050
Dated to within ± 150 years. The next known eruptions date from the early 19th century. 1858
Starting from the upper part of the northern fissure zone, a flow reached the west coast, very close to Moroni. In 1860, another flow again reached the shore near the capital. 1903
Gas emissions in August killed 17 people, according to accounts of the time. 1918
With that of 2005, one of the two most explosive known eruptions of Karthala (Volcanic Explosivity Index 3). 1972
From 8 September to 5 October, lava poured from four fissures in the caldera and covered about 2.5 km². 1977
In April, a fissure opened on the south-western flank. The flow crossed the coastal village of Singani and destroyed about 300 houses. 1991

h: An explosion and a new lake
x: A phreatic explosion in July, caused by groundwater meeting the heat of the volcano. A lake then formed on the floor of the Choungou Chahalé. April 2005
A phreatomagmatic eruption from 16 April. Thousands of residents were evacuated, ash contaminated water and soil, and the crater lake disappeared. November 2005
An explosive eruption from 24 November to 8 December. Ash fell over much of the island, including Moroni, and contaminated many rainwater tanks. May 2006
On 28 May, a magmatic eruption in the Choungou Chahalé: the glow was visible from the coast. The lava lake solidified in early June. January 2007
On 13 January, around 3 am, an eruption of about 12 hours, without strong explosions, formed a lava lake in the crater. A seismic crisis followed, with earthquakes above magnitude 4. May 2012
Residents of Mde and Mkazi reported a glow at the summit on the night of 9–10 May. No eruption was confirmed. 2022

From 15 July, the Observatory recorded abnormal earthquakes under the western flank, up to 50 a day. On 17 August, the Ministry of the Interior raised the yellow alert: climbing was banned. By early October, activity had clearly decreased. No eruption occurred. Dates and figures come from the sources listed at the bottom of the page. The number of people evacuated in 2005 varies between sources (from 2,000 to more than 10,000 in April); we only keep what they agree on. Monitoring

The volcano is monitored by the Karthala Volcano Observatory (OVK) , created in 1988 by the National Centre for Documentation and Scientific Research of the Comoros (CNDRS), with the Institut de physique du globe de Paris (IPGP) and the University of Réunion. Its mission: to monitor the volcano’s activity, develop research, inform the public about volcanic risk and pass alerts on to the authorities in the event of an eruption. The OVK works closely with the Piton de la Fournaise Volcano Observatory on Réunion, which provides technical support. It was thanks to this network that the slight increase in seismicity in early January 2007 announced the eruption of 13 January.

Earthquakes : a network of seismic stations around the massif records the small tremors caused by rising magma or moving fluids. It is the first sign of an awakening. Ground deformation : tiltmeters installed in a lava tube, levelling benchmarks in the caldera and GPS measurements show the volcano “inflating” as magma accumulates. Gases : since 2023, stations have measured carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), an invisible gas that can escape from the volcano.

The European HATARI project (“danger” in Swahili), run from 2021 to 2023 by IPGP, the Piton de la Fournaise Observatory, the CNDRS and OVK, the University of Réunion and the Cité du Volcan, funded new seismic, GNSS (precision GPS) and CO 2 stations, as well as training for Comorian and Réunionese students. In 2024, a relay station was built in the caldera, with the support of UNDP, the World Bank and the Directorate General of Civil Security, to transmit data in real time over 4G. A fragile network. In 2022, only 4 of the 7 stations were working: cables, batteries, solar panels and GPS units had been stolen or destroyed. These instruments protect the island’s inhabitants. If you see a damaged station during the climb, do not touch it and tell your guide. Alert

The OVK informs the authorities; the alert is raised by the Ministry of the Interior, in charge of civil security, under the specialised Karthala emergency plan. The Directorate General of Civil Security then coordinates the response with the Comoros Red Crescent and partners.
Normal volcanic activity. Trips go ahead depending on the weather.
Abnormal activity, with no certain eruption. People are asked to avoid any activity around the volcano. No trips.
Eruption possible in the short term: rescue services and evacuations are prepared. No trips.

Eruption under way or imminent: evacuation of threatened areas. No trips. Only the yellow level is described precisely in the public statements consulted; the orange and red levels are summarised from the Red Crescent’s 2022 action plan. In the event of an alert, follow official instructions only.
Slow, they leave time to evacuate, but destroy roads and houses, as in Singani in 1977.
Carried by the wind, it pollutes water in rainwater tanks, as in 2005.
CO 2 , invisible and heavier than air, collects in hollows: a deadly danger near the volcano.
Tremors that threaten buildings, and mudflows when rain washes away the ash.

When groundwater meets the heat of the magma, as in 1991. In 2022, the OVK estimated that four regions of Grande Comore were exposed, Mbadjini, Hambou, Bambao and Itsandra: 115 villages and nearly 300,000 inhabitants. And our trips?

h: What this means when you climb
x: Yellow level or above: no trips. We follow the statements of the OVK and the Ministry of the Interior; the trip is postponed or refunded under the terms of sale. Never a bivouac in the caldera. Carbon dioxide can collect there, especially at night and in hollows. The French authorities strongly advise their nationals against it; our camp is always set up outside the caldera. At the caldera rim , we keep away from the walls, which can collapse, and we never go down into the craters. No eruption has been confirmed since 2007: the risks of a trip are mostly those of the mountain: cold, fog, rain and falls. Safety: the Go, Adapt, No Go rule

h: Stories and legends of Mount Karthala
x: For the people of Grande Comore, Karthala is not just a volcano: it is a place of memory, stories and spirits. Oral tradition

The most widespread legend links Karthala to King Solomon (Suleiman) and the Queen of Sheba (Balqis), figures found in both the Bible and the Quran. It is told in several versions, depending on the village and the storyteller: Solomon is said to have imprisoned malicious djinns on Grande Comore. In revenge, they stole the wedding ring he had given the Queen of Sheba, engraved with the hundredth name of God and giving power over the djinns, and threw it onto the top of the mountain: its fall opened the huge crater; in another version, Solomon and Balqis spent their honeymoon at the top of Karthala, where the queen dropped her ring into the crater, promising to come back; other tales say the crater was born from the queen’s throne, lost in the archipelago. Comorian writers often return to these wonders, placing the kingdom of the djinns between Karthala and the mountains of Hadramaut, in Y

In Comorian culture, which is Muslim, the mountain, the forest and certain isolated places are traditionally associated with djinns, the spirits of the invisible world. According to some tales, the djinns driven out by Solomon were the first inhabitants of the volcanic islands, before people arrived. These beliefs partly explain the respect, and sometimes the fear, that the summit still inspires. Memory of the eruptions

In April 1977, a fissure opened on the south-western flank of the volcano. The lava flowed down to the coastal village of Singani and destroyed about 300 houses. According to later accounts, the mosque, built of stone, remained standing in the middle of the flow. The black, cooled lava still marks the village landscape.

In November 2005, Moroni woke up under a layer of grey ash. Water in the tanks that collect rain from the roofs became undrinkable. Many people on Grande Comore remember those weeks. All the major eruptions The names of the volcano

The volcano is written Karthala, Kartala or Kartola; in Arabic, القرطالة ( Al Qirtālah ). Grande Comore is called Ngazidja in Shikomori. The two large summit craters have Comorian names: Choungou Chahalé in the centre, Choungou Changomeni to the north. The massif is reached from several regions of the island: Bambao, Dimani, Hambou and Badjini. Some place names on the massif date from colonial times, such as la Convalescence. Explorers and naturalists

The first ascent documented by a European dates from 1863. At the end of the 19th century, the French naturalist Léon Humblot , who had been granted a large part of the land of Grande Comore, sent specimens of the island’s wildlife to European museums. Two endemic birds still bear his name: Humblot’s flycatcher and Humblot’s sunbird. According to local historians, the first roads to the massif were opened at that time, partly with forced labour. Living memory

Discovermores guides grew up at the foot of the volcano. During the climb, they tell the stories of their villages and the names of the places you pass. We are starting to collect them, with everyone’s consent, to publish them here. In the Comoros, this memory has a home: the National Centre for Documentation and Scientific Research (CNDRS) , founded in Moroni in 1979, houses the National Museum, the National Archives and Library, laboratories for oral traditions, archaeology and Arab-Muslim civilisation, and the Karthala Volcano Observatory. Its collections are the reference for anyone who wants to go further.
A tale, a place name, a memory of an eruption passed down in your family: write to us. Every story published is credited to the person who told it. Share a story
Showing Karthala without damaging it: that is the condition for being able to keep showing it. Our rules
Six rules, repeated at the briefing of every trip.
The high heathland recovers very slowly.
Packaging, bottles, food scraps: nothing stays up there.
No plants, no flowers, no stones.
No noise or light towards the birds, no feeding the animals.
Say hello, and ask before photographing people.
An adapted or postponed trip protects the group and the site. Optional

A contribution is suggested with every booking. It is optional and added to the price of the tour. The suggested amount depends mainly on how much the 4×4 is used: the calculation is explained below. It is neither a tax nor a carbon offset. Contributions are pooled in a fund. During the trips, the guides pick up the litter found along the route. Each batch is weighed, photographed and tracked to its final destination, then recorded in the data space. Several times a year, clean-up days bring together volunteers, young people and partners on the busiest areas. Support an action Method

The rules that apply to every trip booked with Discovermores. This English translation is provided for convenience. In case of any difference, the French version prevails.
These terms apply to trips to the Karthala volcano organised by Discovermores SARL (RC No. 8563-B-18, Moroni, Union of the Comoros) and presented on karthala360.discovermores.com.

The tours, their content and prices are described on the Tours page. Prices are given in euros. Payment in Comorian francs is accepted at the fixed rate of €1 = 491.96775 KMF. Zero Effort and Soft Trek are sold at a flat rate for 1 to 4 people, with a supplement per person beyond that. The Volcano Bivouac and the Full Climb are sold per person.

A request sent through the website or WhatsApp commits neither the customer nor Discovermores. The booking becomes firm once Discovermores has confirmed it in writing and the deposit has been received.

Deposit on confirmation: 30% of the total price. Balance: no later than the day before the trip, or on the day itself before departure. Accepted payment methods: Virement bancaire, PayPal, MVola or Wakati. PayPal also lets you pay by bank card, without a PayPal account. Details and instructions are on the Pay for your booking page. A receipt is issued for every payment.
The contribution offered at booking is optional. It is paid into the Karthala360 action fund and used for environmental actions around Karthala. It is refunded if Discovermores cancels the trip.

More than 7 days before the trip: full refund of the sums paid. Between 7 days and 72 hours before: the deposit is kept. You may also postpone the trip once, free of charge, within 6 months. Less than 72 hours before, or no-show at departure: the sums paid are kept. Any cancellation must be made in writing (WhatsApp or email).

Safety comes before the programme. If Discovermores decides on a No Go (weather, state of the track or trail, volcanic alert, insufficient supervision), the customer chooses between a new date, free of charge, and a full refund of the sums paid. If the trip is adapted on site (time, route, pace, turning back before the summit) for safety reasons, no refund is due once the trip has started. If Discovermores replaces the tour before departure with a cheaper one, the difference is refunded.

Minimum age: 5 for Zero Effort, 8 for Soft Trek, 12 for the Bivouac and 15 for the Full Climb. Minors take part under the responsibility of an adult who is present. Each participant fills in the registration form and reports any health problem that could affect the trip. They follow the guide’s instructions. The guide may refuse departure, or stop a participant’s climb, if their safety or that of the group requires it.

Discovermores professional liability insurance: Amana Assurances, Moroni, Union of the Comoros, policy no. [À COMPLÉTER : Amana Assurances policy number] . This insurance does not replace personal insurance. For visitors from abroad, travel insurance covering mountain hiking and repatriation is strongly recommended.
Consent to appear in published photos is requested at registration. Refusing has no consequence on the trip. Anyone may ask at any time for a photo of themselves to be removed.
